pages.text: You do not evolve by wanting to. You evolve by living a certain way for long enough that the next step becomes obvious.$(br2)Satisfy enough of the list and you will know. There is always one final act - something you have never done before - that turns readiness into change.
$(l)A note on failure:$() you will make things you did not mean to make. Hold on to them. Most of human history is people doing something wrong in a way that turned out to be useful.

Losing every last one of your band is how a line ends - but rarely all at once. Lose three bands and your kind dies out, and what is left of it is an older, poorer form of the same animal: $(l)anamensis$() behind Australopithecus, $(l)rudolfensis$() beside habilis, $(l)ergaster$() behind erectus.

A fallback asks less of you - one hard requirement and two of four - and its road leads straight back to what you fell from.$(br2)Lose two bands there and there is nothing further to fall to. Your line is finished.$(br2)These cousins are out there in any case: you will meet bands of them whether or not you have ever been one.

$(l)Extra effort$() (a world setting, off by default) turns the fallbacks into rungs rather than a net. With it on, habilis reaches erectus only by way of ergaster - the long way, through every form your line actually passed through.
